title: Magnus Carlsen Modern-family games as Black
purpose: Source material for a Magnus Modern training tab in Trey's Chess Coach AI app. Trey is about 1760 Lichess rapid and plays the Modern as Black.

games.notes: Carlsen's knight went f6-h5 rather than a standard ...Bg7 Modern. Adams later broke with f4 and finished with 38.Rxh6+. Black resigned. TWIC notes this is the Gerard Welling / Tony Miles 'North Sea' idea.

plan_positions.plan: With ...a6, ...b5 and ...Bb7 already in place, strike the centre immediately with ...c5 against White's e5 wedge.
Do not panic about the pawn wedged on e6. Keep developing, meet a4 with ...b4, and take the a-pawn.
Ignore the hanging kingside pawn and go after White's king: ...Qxa2, then ...Na4 and ...Qxb2+.
The Hippo is complete (pawns on a6/b6/d6/e6/g6/h6, knights on d7/e7, bishop on b7). Expand on the kingside with ...g5, gaining space and preparing later piece activity.
After exchanging on d3, start a queenside raid with ...Qa5, heading for ...Qb4 and pressure against b2.
White has sacrificed an exchange with h4-h5 and Rxh5. Close the centre with ...e6/...d5 if needed, then break with ...c5 against the long-castled king.
Against the Austrian-style f4 setup, switch to the Gurgenidze plan: ...c6 and ...d5, fixing the centre, with ...h5 to come.
In the Pirc Austrian Attack, challenge the big centre at once with ...c5.
In this ...c6 Modern/Pirc with the queen already on a5, strike in the centre with ...e5, then use the queen on the queenside (...Qb4) and a later ...b5 expansion.

Carlsen's chosen plan was the piece sacrifice 10...Bxg4, aiming for two pawns and an attack after White's g4. It did not yield enough compensation and he lost. Include this as a cautionary 'what plan did he choose?' position, not as a model to copy uncritically.

white_systems.how_he_responded: In the Pirc, the standard ...c5 break (Mamedov 2018; also ...c5 vs 5.Bd3 against Polgar 2012). In the Modern, either the Tiger ...a6/...b5/...c5 plan (Wei Yi 2016) or a Gurgenidze ...c6/...d5 clamp (Tari and Christiansen 2021).

white_systems.system: 150 Attack (Be3, Qd2, often long castling or h4)
white_systems.how_he_responded: The Tiger move ...a6 and ...b5. Vs Erigaisi's Qd2/f3/O-O-O he closed the h-file with ...h5, met e5 with ...b4, and attacked the king (...Qa4-xa2-xb2). Vs Pragg's 5.h4 he allowed the Rxh5 sacrifice and countered with ...e6, ...d5 and ...c5.

white_systems.system: Be3 with a4, restraining ...b5, sometimes g4
white_systems.how_he_responded: Against Naiditsch he still played ...a6, then ...Nf6 and 7...e5, and later tried 10...Bxg4. The sacrifice failed. a4 is a real problem for the Tiger ...b5 plan.
Tiger ...a6/...b5 vs Perelshteyn, absorbing 7.e5 and 8.e6. Vs Zhigalko, a ...c6 Modern/Pirc with ...Qa5 and an ...e5 break. Vs Tomashevsky, a Hippo after White's a4 stopped a quick ...b5.

white_systems.system: Early e5 space push, including the e6 wedge
white_systems.how_he_responded: Meet e5 with ...Bb7 and ...c5 (Wei Yi), or sit behind an e6 wedge and take on a4 (Perelshteyn), or use ...b4 and a king attack if White has castled long (Erigaisi).
Vs 5.h4 (Pragg) he allowed Rxh5 and counterbroke in the centre. Vs 6.g4 (Pranesh) he answered 6...h5. Vs 7.g4 (Naiditsch) he played ...e5 and later sacrificed on g4, unsuccessfully.

An experimental sideline, not his main Modern. Classical loss to Adams (2010). Blitz win vs Savchenko (2010, White took on h5). Blitz loss vs Chadaev after 3...Nxe4 (2012). Better treated as a surprise weapon with mixed results.
Completed the double-fianchetto Hippo (...b6, ...e6, ...Ne7, ...Nd7, ...Bb7, ...h6), then expanded with ...g5. White's later e5 was dangerous, but Carlsen found tactical resources and won the ending.

gaps: No well-documented elite game was found of Carlsen as Black in a pure 1.d4 g6 2.c4 A41/A42 Modern that does not transpose to a King's Indian (early ...Nf6) or to an e4-Modern (White playing 2.e4). Several listed '1.d4 g6' games (Wei Yi, Perelshteyn, Tomashevsky) transposed after 2.e4.
No verified 1.c4 g6 Modern game (staying in English/Modern rather than a KID or Grünfeld) was located in this pass.

A ChessBase course chapter is titled '4.c4 e5 5.Nc3 exd4: Firouzja vs Carlsen', implying 1.e4 g6 2.d4 Bg7 3.Nf3 d6 4.c4 e5. No public PGN or event details for that exact Modern game were found. The well-known Firouzja-Carlsen World Blitz 2019 game is a Ruy Lopez (1.e4 e5), not a Modern, and must not be used as a substitute.
Savchenko-Carlsen 2010: game metadata is confirmed on chessgames.com, but the PGN comes only from a secondary blog attributing ChessBase. It was not retrieved from TWIC or chessmoments.

Mamedov-Carlsen 2018: 51-move draw and B09 Austrian Attack are confirmed by TWIC, ChessBase, historicchessgames and chessmoments; the move list is from a contemporaneous ChessTalk transcription. The official TWIC zip could not be downloaded (server 406).
Polgar-Carlsen 2012: confirmed as the UNAM blindfold final game (Chess.com). The PGN is a public secondary move list, not a raw TWIC file.
This is a curated set of notable games, not a complete census. Carlsen has many more online blitz Modern games (Titled Tuesday and similar) that were not exhaustively collected.
The Hippo sample at a high over-the-board level is essentially one game (Tomashevsky, World Rapid 2022).
Third-party opening-stat pages (for example claims of hundreds of Carlsen Modern games and a high win percentage) were not independently audited and are not used as facts here.

annotations.text: The knight goes to h5 instead of a …Bg7 Modern. TWIC notes the Gerard Welling / Tony Miles North Sea idea. Treat this as a historical experiment.
Adams breaks with f4. This is a classical game, and Carlsen lost it.
38.Rxh6+. Carlsen resigned.

The same 3.e5 Nh5 idea as against Adams, here in a World Blitz game. The event and the 0-1 result are confirmed. The move list is a secondary score, so read the moves with more caution than the TWIC games.
White takes on h5. Carlsen won the blitz game.
A sharper Norwegian cousin: the knight takes on e4. A short blitz loss, useful as a warning.
White's f-pawn reaches f5. The game is overrun after f4–f5.
Blindfold, not a classical game. Against the Austrian Attack he meets 4.f4 with an early …c5.
After the trade on d3, the queen starts a raid toward b4 and b2.
The queen steps to b4, still heading for the b-pawn.
The queen takes on b2, and a passed b-pawn follows. He won the blindfold game.
He still plays …a6, the Tiger move.
5.a4 stops …b5. That is the limit of the expansion plan in this game.
White expands with 7.g4.
With …b5 stopped, he strikes in the centre with …e5.
He sacrifices the bishop on g4. The attack was not enough: Naiditsch won, and later promoted the a-pawn. A warning, not a model to copy.
Tiger Modern: …a6, ready for …b5. Chess.com reported that he chose the Modern in the style advocated by Tiger Hillarp Persson.
White allowed …b5. That is the characteristic queenside expansion.
White pushes e5. The reply in this game is concrete: the bishop is already on b7, and …c5 comes next.
With …a6, …b5 and …Bb7 in place, …c5 strikes the e5 centre. The queens come off soon after.
Chess.com reported that the first 18 moves were still theory. A long queenless ending follows.
The game was decided after 48…Nc5, which Wei Yi missed. Carlsen won.
The same …a6 idea as against Wei Yi.
…b5 follows. White has not stopped it.
White jams a pawn onto e6. He keeps developing around the wedge.
…Nf8, then …Qd7 and …Nf6, developing around the pawn on e6.
12.a4 is met by …b4.
The queen takes the a-pawn. He won the ending.

Pirc, Austrian Attack. The early plan is …c5. Yermolinsky (ChessBase) wrote that this Pirc “worked out well enough to equalize easily,” and that it left little to play for a win. Drawn. The move list is a ChessTalk transcription, not a TWIC file.
Gurgenidze family: …c6, rather than a pure …Bg7 Modern. Online rapid.
Against f4 he clamps the centre with …d5.
Then …h5, before White's space on the kingside grows.
34…Qf1 invades. He won the ending.
Same day as Tari, and the same shell: …c6, …d5, then …h5.
Here the later break is …c5. Drawn in a long rook ending.
150 Attack. Robert Ris (ChessBase) discussed this Generation Cup Modern with 4…a6. This is the prelim, not the later final. Online rapid.
…b5 is allowed.
White has castled long and pushed the h-pawn. …h5 meets that pawn.
9.e5 is met by …b4.
The queen heads for the white king: …Qa4, then …Qxa2 and …Qxb2+.
19.Bxg6 is ignored. The queen takes on a2.
21…Qxb2+. He won.
Same event. 150 Attack with 5.h4, after …a6.
6.h5 and Rxh5 is the exchange sacrifice. Ris wrote that it was close to winning for White, and that Pragg let Carlsen off the hook.
He keeps the centre closed, starting with …e6.
…d5 follows.
Then …c5 against the long-castled king. Drawn in a bare-king ending.
5.a4 stops a quick …b5, so he builds a Hippo. Over-the-board rapid. ChessBase (Igor Stohl) presented this as a model Hippo. It is the one Hippo game in this set.
The shell: …b6, then …e6, …Ne7, …Nd7, …Bb7 and …h6. Pawns end up on a6, b6, d6, e6, g6 and h6.
The Hippo is complete. He expands with …g5.
17.e5 is dangerous. The game was saved by tactics, not by a quiet retreat.
He plays …axb5.
Then …Bxe5. The win came from those tactics and the ending, not from a painless opening edge.
A classical …c6 Modern, in the same family as the Gurgenidze games.
Queenside expansion with …b5.
6.g4 is met by …h5.
He closes the centre with …d5 after g4–g5.
A late …c5 shows up in the defensive scramble. It was not the original plan. Drawn after a sharp attack.
Online blitz, 3+1. …c6, and the queen comes to a5. A clean illustration, and still blitz.
With the queen already on a5, …e5 is the central break.
The queen moves to b4 and keeps the pressure on the queenside.
Then …b5.

wei-yi-c5-break.text: Bring the knight out and castle before touching the centre.
With …a6, …b5 and …Bb7 already in, strike the e5 pawn with …c5.
Take on e5 at once and open the long diagonal.

perelshteyn-b4-qxa4.text: Stay under the pawn on e6. Meet a4 with …b4 and take the a-pawn with the queen.
Spend the next moves only on getting the king to safety.
Trade the light-squared bishop for the knight on g5 and simplify.

erigaisi-qxa2-attack.text: Drop a piece back and hold the kingside.
Trade queens and play an endgame.
Ignore the kingside and take on a2, then hunt the king with …Na4 and …Qxb2+.

tomashevsky-g5-hippo.text: The Hippo is complete. Expand on the kingside with …g5.
Castle and keep every pawn on the sixth rank.

polgar-qa5-raid.text: Chip the d5 pawn with …e6 and open the centre.
Start a queenside raid with the queen, toward b4 and the pawn on b2.
Trade rooks on the c-file and head for a simplified ending.

pragg-c5-vs-exchange-sac.text: Castle kingside and try to hold the extra material quietly.
Take on e5 and open lines while the king is still uncastled.
The centre is already closed with …e6 and …d5. Break with …c5 against the long-castled king.

tari-gurgenidze-d5.text: Fianchetto the bishop and castle into the pawn centre.
Against f4, clamp the centre with …d5. …h5 comes next. This is the Gurgenidze plan.

mamedov-austrian-c5.text: Castle first, and only later choose between …c5 and …e5.
Switch to …c6 and …d5, a Gurgenidze clamp.
In the Pirc Austrian Attack, challenge the centre at once with …c5.

zhigalko-e5-break.text: Develop the queen's knight and wait for White to commit.
The queen is already on a5. Strike with …e5, then use the queen on the queenside and a later …b5.

naiditsch-bxg4-sacrifice.text: Develop the queen's knight and leave the pawn on g4 alone.
Sacrifice the bishop on g4, aiming for two pawns and an attack.
Take on d5 with the knight and keep the dark-squared bishop.

themes.title: Tiger …a6 / …b5
themes.body: In the serious games in this set, the characteristic Modern is …a6 and, when White allows it, …b5, with …c5 or …e5 later. Chess.com tied the Wei Yi game to Tiger Hillarp Persson. Naiditsch shows the limit: 5.a4 stops …b5, and the later sacrifice on g4 failed.

themes.title: When to play …c5
themes.body: …c5 is how he challenges a broad white centre, often after a piece or a queenside pawn is ready. Immediate in the Pirc Austrian against Mamedov, and early against Polgar. After …a6/…b5/…Bb7 against Wei Yi. After Rxh5 against Praggnanandhaa. Later, inside a Gurgenidze, against Christiansen. Against Pranesh it appears late, during the defensive scramble.

themes.title: The …e5 break
themes.body: When the position is more like a Pirc, or when …b5 has been stopped, he also uses …e5. Against Naiditsch that is 7…e5, after 7.g4 and 5.a4. Against Zhigalko it is 8…e5 with the queen already on a5. Mamedov and Polgar are …c5 games.

themes.title: A big centre, and the e6 wedge
themes.body: White's space is met with a concrete reply. Wei Yi: …Bb7 and …c5 against e5. Perelshteyn: develop around an e6 wedge with …Nf8, …Qd7 and …Nf6, then take on a4. Erigaisi: …b4, then a queen raid, after White has castled long. Tomashevsky: 17.e5 was dangerous and needed …axb5 and …Bxe5. Praggnanandhaa: …d5 kept the centre closed, then …c5.

themes.title: Gurgenidze …c6 and …d5
themes.body: A second branch, useful against an f4 centre. Tari and Christiansen play …c6, …d5 and …h5; Christiansen later breaks with …c5, Tari invades with 34…Qf1. Pranesh plays …c6 and …b5, and …d5 only after g4–g5. Zhigalko plays …c6 without an early …d5, then …Qa5 and …e5. A plan B when White smashes f4 and e5.

themes.title: Hippo, then …g5
themes.body: The over-the-board Hippo in this set is one game: Tomashevsky, World Rapid 2022. After 5.a4 stopped a quick …b5, he built the Hippo — pawns on a6, b6, d6, e6, g6 and h6, knights on d7 and e7, bishop on b7 — and expanded with 11…g5. Stohl presented it as a model. The later win came from tactics and the ending. Use it as a flexible backup when …b5 is restrained.

themes.title: Pawn storms and opposite-side attacks
themes.body: Erigaisi is the 150 Attack model: …h5, then …Qa4, …Qxa2 and …Qxb2+, ignoring 19.Bxg6. Praggnanandhaa is the model for living with Rxh5: …e6, …d5, …c5. Pranesh meets 6.g4 with …h5. Naiditsch's 10…Bxg4 is what he chose, and the attack failed.

themes.title: The Norwegian experiment
themes.body: 1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6, and then 3.e5 Nh5 or 3.Nf3 Nxe4, is in the documented record. The structure is different from a usual Modern. Classical loss to Adams. Blitz win against Savchenko, whose move list is a secondary score. Blitz loss to Chadaev after 3…Nxe4. Keep it as history.

study.footer: Left out on purpose: no verified game of Carlsen as Black in a pure 1.d4 g6 2.c4 Modern, no verified 1.c4 g6 Modern, and no public PGN for a ChessBase chapter headed Firouzja–Carlsen in the Modern (the well-known 2019 World Blitz game is a Ruy Lopez). This is a curated set, not a census. The over-the-board Hippo sample here is one game.
